_note: Safety is the nurse in the field and the patient in trouble: visit check-in timers, panic with a time-bound live location, patient SOS, next-of-kin nomination and alerting, safeguarding reports, Sentinel deviations at tiers one to three, and the security incident register the identity service already keeps. Wave 2 contract; Waves 3 to 5 build.

refusals.statement: Nothing is dispatched without a human, except for an unresponsive patient or an SOS.
refusals.why: High specificity for dispatching paramedics; a human confirms (§13).

refusals.statement: A consumer wearable alone never raises dispatch.
refusals.why: BYO signals guide conversation; certified devices carry clinical weight.

refusals.statement: Next of kin see plain language, never clinical detail.

refusals.statement: Live location is shared for a fixed window, and the window always ends.
refusals.why: A share with no end is a tracker.

refusals.statement: The window is the one the desk's policy sets. A phone does not choose how long it is watched.
refusals.why: packages/catalog/field-safety.json declares panic.windowMinutes. A caller-chosen window is a share whose end is whatever was sent.

refusals.statement: A panic goes to the desk. Nobody is sent to it until a person at the desk decides.
refusals.why: §13: never auto-dispatch without a human. The exceptions are an unresponsive patient and an SOS, and a nurse's panic is neither.

routes.summary: Read the field-safety timings in force, the range an admin may set each within, and every change made to them.

response.why: The version in force. A change is made against it, and a visit or a panic that starts now keeps it.
Each timing: its id, unit, the minutes in force, its default, and the lowest and highest an admin may set.
Every accepted change, oldest first: who, when, from, to and why. Nothing in it is edited or removed.

refusals.statement: Only an admin reads the field-safety settings and who changed them.
refusals.why: The history names the people who changed how long the desk waits. It is read by the role that can change it, as the incident register is.

withdrawn.why: Its rows carried the four field-safety timings in minutes and nothing else. A Safety setting that is on or off, or a list of roles, cannot be read through it, and packages/catalog/settings.json gives every engine's settings one read route, with each setting's provenance, limits and review. Version two is that route.

routes.summary: Change one field-safety timing, with a reason, against the version in force. It applies to visits and panics that start after it.

request.why: Chosen by the caller. The same key twice is the same change once, and the history gains one row.
grace, panic-window, extension-steps or extension-ceiling, from packages/catalog/field-safety.json settings.timings.
The new value, for a timing that is one number of minutes.
The new extension steps, smallest first, for extension-steps.
Why. Asked for by the handler rather than the binder, so that a change without one is refused in its own sentence rather than the general one for a missing field.
The settings version the admin was looking at. A change against an older one is refused.

response.why: When it took effect. A visit or a panic that started before this keeps the version it started under.

refusals.statement: Only an admin changes a field-safety setting.
refusals.why: These timings decide how long the desk waits before it looks for a nurse. The admin role in packages/catalog/vetting.json changes them, and the change is recorded against a named person; a nurse, the desk and every engine only read them.

refusals.statement: There is no field-safety setting by that name.
refusals.why: An unknown setting is refused rather than stored, or the history fills with changes nothing reads.

refusals.statement: A change to a field-safety setting says why, or it is not made.
refusals.why: The history is read after something has gone wrong. A change with no reason is a number somebody moved.

refusals.statement: These settings changed after you opened them. Read what is in force now and decide against that.
refusals.why: Two admins changing one timing from screens opened at the same time would each overwrite a decision they never saw.

refusals.statement: No field-safety timing is set to zero or less, whatever its range says.
refusals.why: A grace of nothing pages the desk the moment a visit is due to end, and a panic window of nothing shows a nurse's position to nobody. The range is a proposal and could be set wrongly; this refusal does not depend on it.

refusals.statement: That is outside the range an admin may set for this setting.
refusals.why: The lowest and highest sit beside the default in packages/catalog/field-safety.json. Moving a timing past them is a change to that contract, not a setting.

refusals.statement: Extension steps are listed from the smallest to the largest, each once.
refusals.why: The steps are the buttons a nurse presses at a door. Two the same, or an order that jumps about, is a choice she has to stop and read.

refusals.statement: No extension step can be larger than the most a visit may be extended.
refusals.why: A step the ceiling never lets a nurse take is a button that is always refused.

refusals.statement: That is already the value in force, so there is nothing to change.
refusals.why: A change that changes nothing is a row in the history saying something happened when nothing did.

routes.emitsNoneBecause: No engine acts on a change to Safety's timings. Core does not read them, because Safety sends the deadline on what it raises, and the event contract refuses an event nobody subscribes to. A change is the row it appends to Safety's own history, which GET /v1/safety/settings@1 reads, and it reaches the next visit and the next panic through the settings in force.

withdrawn.why: It carried a timing as minutes or stepMinutes and nothing else, so a Safety setting that is on or off, or a list of roles, cannot be changed through it. Version two is the change route packages/catalog/settings.json gives every engine, carrying every type with the shared refusal sentences.

routes.summary: Change one field-safety setting, with a reason, against the version in force. It applies to the visits, panics and changes that start after it.

request.why: Chosen by the caller. The same key twice is the same change once, and the history gains one row.
The setting's key, from the settings block of the engine's own contract.
The new value, for a setting in minutes, a count, cents or a percentage.
The new value, for a setting that is on or off.
The new value, for a setting that is one of a few named choices.
The new wording, for a setting patients or nurses read.
The new roles, for a setting that names roles from packages/catalog/vetting.json.
The new rota, for a setting that is windows of a post, days and hours. A post, never a named person.
The new values, for a setting that is a list.
The new values, for a setting whose parts change together.
Why. Asked for by the handler rather than the binder, so that a change without one is refused in its own sentence rather than the general one for a missing field.
The settings version the admin was looking at. A change against an older one is refused.

response.why: When it took effect. Whatever started before it keeps the version it started under.

refusals.statement: Only the role a setting names changes it, and the change is recorded against a named person.
refusals.why: A setting decides how the platform treats people. The role or capability the setting names changes it, and a change is recorded against somebody who can be asked about it; everybody else only reads what is in force.

refusals.statement: There is no setting by that name.
refusals.why: An unknown setting is refused rather than stored, or the history fills with changes nothing reads.

refusals.statement: A change to a setting says why, or it is not made.
refusals.why: The history is read after something has gone wrong. A change with no reason is a number somebody moved.

refusals.statement: These settings changed after you opened them. Read what is in force now and decide against that.
refusals.why: Two admins changing one setting from screens opened at the same time would each overwrite a decision they never saw.

refusals.statement: That is not the kind of value this setting holds.
refusals.why: A word where a number belongs, or a list where one choice belongs, is a guess at what the admin meant, and a setting is never set by a guess.

refusals.statement: This setting is never nought or less, whatever its range says.
refusals.why: A wait of nothing, an offer that lapses as it is made and a fee of nothing are never what anybody meant. The range is a proposal and could be set wrongly; this refusal does not depend on it.

refusals.statement: Every role a setting names is a role on the vetting register.
refusals.why: A role the register does not hold is a gate nobody can be vetted through, which looks like a shortage rather than a mistake.

refusals.statement: That wording is longer than this setting allows.
refusals.why: The maximum is the space the words are read in. Wording that does not fit is cut off where somebody reads it.

refusals.statement: That wording drops a sentence this setting must always keep.
refusals.why: Some wording carries a promise that protects somebody. It may be reworded around that sentence and never without it.

refusals.statement: That rota leaves hours uncovered that must always have somebody on them.
refusals.why: A rota with a gap is an alert with nobody to go to, and nobody finds out until one arrives.

refusals.statement: That is outside what an admin may set for this setting.
refusals.why: The bounds, the allowed values and the allowed roles sit beside the default in the engine's contract. Moving a setting past them is a change to that contract, not a setting.

refusals.statement: That is already the value in force, so there is nothing to change.
refusals.why: A change that changes nothing is a row in the history saying something happened when nothing did.

refusals.statement: Extension steps are listed from the smallest to the largest, each once.
refusals.why: The steps are the buttons a nurse presses at a door. Two the same, or an order that jumps about, is a choice she has to stop and read.

refusals.statement: No extension step can be larger than the most a visit may be extended.
refusals.why: A step the ceiling never lets a nurse take is a button that is always refused.

routes.emitsNoneBecause: No engine acts on a settings change. The engine that owns a setting reads the value in force when it starts something, and the event contract refuses an event nobody subscribes to. A change is the row it appends to the engine's own history, which the read route returns.
